articles.title: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.description: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology The Oakland Press
articles.description_html: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology  The Oakland Press
articles.article_title: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.heading: Oakland Schools builds AI strategy as educators navigate promise, pitfalls of new technology
articles.summary: Only 30% of teens in the survey said they had discussed AI safety with a teacher, and just 27% said they had discussed AI literacy.
articles.content:
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly woven into students’ schoolwork and teachers’ daily routines, Oakland Schools is taking a more deliberate approach: Teach educators how to use the technology, help districts develop policies and keep humans at the center of education.
That effort is being led by Justin Bruno, director of AI Strategy and Innovation at Oakland Schools, who was hired in September 2025 to help develop an all-encompassing strategy for artificial intelligence.
“I think that was evidence of Oakland Schools making this a priority,” Bruno said. “Trying to figure out what sorts of strategies we need to be setting internally around AI, and how that’s going to fit into our operations, and how we do things.”
Bruno recently added Shana Ramin from Royal Oak as an AI consultant to his team, who will work directly with local school districts to help them plan, implement and strategize around emerging challenges and opportunities.
The work comes as schools across Oakland County and the country grapple with a technology that students are already using.
Common Sense Media, an independent non-profit education research group, released a study in August that asked more than 1,000 U.S. students between 13 and 17 years old about how they use AI. Seventy percent said they use AI for schoolwork, and nearly two-thirds of those students said they use it in ways that can shift critical thinking from the students to the technology.
Among teens who use AI for schoolwork, 63% said they get an answer from AI in at least one way: 35% said they get an answer and then fix or improve it based on what they know; 31% said they get an answer and rewrite it to sound like themselves, and 25% said they use an AI-generated answer as-is.
The findings underscore the challenge facing educators. AI is a powerful tool, but it makes it easier for students to bypass the very thinking and practice that assignments are designed to develop.
At the same time, students appear to recognize the trade-offs.
Thirty-eight percent of AI-using teens said the technology leads them to generate fewer of their own ideas, while 39% said they feel they are missing out on learning when they use AI to complete assignments. Yet 66% said AI helps them understand schoolwork, suggesting that students’ experiences with the technology are more complicated than a simple cheating-versus-no-cheating debate.
Common Sense Media cautioned against assuming that students themselves are the primary problem.
“As educators and policymakers weigh risks, we should be cautious about narratives that instinctively blame teens for using AI in schoolwork,” the report said, arguing that schools also need to consider the broader culture and incentives surrounding AI use.
For Oakland Schools, that means focusing on literacy and responsible use rather than relying exclusively on bans.
Training educators to use AI
Oakland Schools has adopted ChatGPT EDU, an education-focused version of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, giving staff access to the tool. Because the organization uses Google Workspace, staff also have access to Gemini, another AI platform.
It is rolling out a monthly webinar series designed to help employees understand what the tools can do and how they might fit into everyday workflows.
Districts have designated professional development days throughout the year, and Oakland Schools is increasingly being asked to provide AI training during those sessions. The agency also plans countywide conferences, sessions and webinars for educators who can attend voluntarily.
Educators might learn how to use AI tools in their daily work, but the sessions also will address instructional questions, such as how a social studies teacher might rethink assessments in an era when students can turn to AI or how educators might use emerging tools to better understand student progress.
“There might be a new AI tool that’s just debuted in the last couple years that might be really helpful,” Bruno said. “We’re trying to build those training initiatives.”
Rather than attempting to deliver every message directly to every educator, Oakland Schools is also working with district-level leaders who can help spread AI guidance.
The approach recognizes that each district is at a different point in its AI journey.
Bruno points to Royal Oak as one of the leaders in the county. Avondale Schools also has taken a proactive approach under the leadership of Michelle Gierman, he said. The district has created a Student AI Advisory Council and regularly has students update district leaders on how they are using AI.
He said Oxford Schools is developing guidance for staff and students while considering questions surrounding AI tools and assessment redesign.
Holly Schools is earlier in the process, but has made AI a priority for the school year. The district recently released guidance for staff and is emphasizing professional development, along with expectations that schools and teachers address digital citizenship and AI literacy with students throughout the year.
“There’s some great stuff happening in the county,” Bruno said.
Moving beyond the chatbot debate
The rapid growth of AI has also created a new education technology market.
Companies such as MagicSchool, SchoolAI and Brisk have emerged as prominent AI-focused tools for K-12 education. Unlike general-purpose AI systems, some of these platforms offer additional guardrails and features designed specifically for schools.
That distinction matters as districts decide how students should access AI.
A district might be comfortable giving older students access to a general-purpose tool such as ChatGPT or Gemini while deciding that younger students need a more controlled environment.
But Bruno said schools ultimately need to think beyond simply deciding which tools students can or cannot use.
“We still want to encourage a systemic change,” he said. “Because when kids go home and do that work, they’re going to have access to tools that everyone has access to that can be used for good or for ill.”
The Common Sense report findings reinforce that concern. Among teens who use AI for schoolwork, 44% said an AI tool had been blocked on a school network or device. Of those students, 59% said they simply switched to a personal device to get around the ban.
The report also found a significant gap in AI literacy education. Only 27% of teens said a teacher had ever talked with them about how to use AI safely, while 73% said they had not.
The report also said blanket bans and one-size-fits-all restrictions can prevent some students from benefiting from technology and urged schools to leave room for accommodations based on individual student needs.
For Bruno, the answer lies in teaching students how to navigate AI rather than assuming they can be shielded from it.
Keeping people at the center
Bruno’s approach is rooted in a broader question: What should AI actually be doing in a school?
Education, he said, is fundamentally human and he sees AI as a way to strengthen work educators are already doing.
“Education is such a human-focused thing, and we don’t want to be automating things that would still benefit from the human being the primary deliverer of or facilitator of that service,” he said. “ So by no means am I thinking we’re going to automate or speed up things. It’s more of how can we use AI to do what we’ve always done better for more people.”
That distinction becomes important when considering AI tools that can grade papers or provide feedback on student writing.
Those tools can help a teacher who is overwhelmed by an ever growing workload and class sizes. But Bruno said schools should be careful not to confuse efficiency with educational effectiveness.
“The expertise of that human and the motivation that that human can provide to improve their writing, or to improve their work over time” remain essential, he said.
An AI system may be able to identify weaknesses in a student’s writing, but a teacher can understand the student behind the writing and provide encouragement, context and motivation that a machine cannot replicate in the same way.
That human relationship is something Bruno said should remain central even as schools adopt increasingly sophisticated technology.
A critical year for AI literacy
The Common Sense study suggests schools have little time to waste in developing AI literacy.
Only 30% of teens in the survey said they had discussed AI safety with a teacher, and just 27% said they had discussed AI literacy. Forty-four percent said they had talked with a teacher about rules governing when they should and should not use AI.
The report characterized the current school year as an important opportunity for teachers to begin those conversations.
Students themselves also identified skills they believe will remain important in the future. Among AI-using teens, 55% identified working well with others as an important future skill, 50% cited fact-checking and critical thinking, and 48% cited reading and understanding complex information.
Those are the kinds of skills educators are trying to protect as AI becomes more capable.
For Oakland Schools, the goal is not simply to keep pace with a rapidly changing technology. It is to help districts make thoughtful decisions about where AI belongs — and where it does not.
As a new department, Bruno said, his team is building on work that was already underway at Oakland Schools before he arrived.
“There was great AI work happening before I came on board,” he said. “Oakland Schools were leading lots of great learning, and so now we’re just kind of accelerating that and trying to be a leader in the state.”
He believes the agency is moving in that direction.
The challenge now is to make sure the technology advances without leaving the people at the heart of education behind.

articles.article_title: Can Cape Cod scientists save the world's coral reefs? They have a few ideas.
articles.heading: Can Cape Cod scientists save the world's coral reefs? They have a few ideas.
articles.summary: Scientists at WHOI's new Schiller Center for Reef Solutions are experimenting with underwater robots, reef soundtracks and new ocean technologies.
articles.content:
OCEANS
Can Cape Cod scientists save the world's coral reefs? They have a few ideas.
Heather McCarron
Cape Cod Times
Aug. 30, 2026, 6:03 a.m. ET
For people who have never slipped on a snorkeling mask and peered down at a coral reef, it can be easy to view reef loss as a faraway problem confined to tropical waters and coastlines far from Cape Cod.
But Amy Apprill, a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution scientist who will lead a newly launched coral reef center in Woods Hole, says the stakes are far broader.

articles.content:
The Manufacturers Life Insurance Company Acquires Shares of 98,847 Amkor Technology, Inc. $AMKR
The Manufacturers Life Insurance Company bought a new stake in Amkor Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMKR - Free Report) during the 2nd quarter, according to its most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The firm bought 98,847 shares of the semiconductor company's stock, valued at approximately $8,524,000.
Other institutional investors have also modified their holdings of the company. BlackRock Inc. acquired a new stake in shares of Amkor Technology during the second quarter worth $1,060,005,000. AQR Capital Management LLC increased its stake in Amkor Technology by 18.4% in the 3rd quarter. AQR Capital Management LLC now owns 4,211,529 shares of the semiconductor company's stock valued at $119,607,000 after buying an additional 653,489 shares during the period. State Street Corp raised its position in Amkor Technology by 1.4% during the 4th quarter. State Street Corp now owns 3,473,925 shares of the semiconductor company's stock worth $137,151,000 after buying an additional 47,514 shares during the last quarter. First Trust Advisors LP raised its position in Amkor Technology by 37.4% during the 4th quarter. First Trust Advisors LP now owns 2,722,310 shares of the semiconductor company's stock worth $107,477,000 after buying an additional 740,701 shares during the last quarter. Finally, Principal Financial Group Inc. lifted its stake in shares of Amkor Technology by 19.3% in the 1st quarter. Principal Financial Group Inc. now owns 2,622,744 shares of the semiconductor company's stock worth $118,107,000 after acquiring an additional 423,629 shares during the period. Institutional investors and hedge funds own 42.76% of the company's stock.
Amkor Technology Stock Down 7.5%
Amkor Technology stock opened at $47.88 on Friday. Amkor Technology, Inc. has a fifty-two week low of $23.36 and a fifty-two week high of $96.68. The firm has a market capitalization of $11.90 billion, a price-to-earnings ratio of 21.47 and a beta of 2.24. The stock's fifty day moving average is $62.52 and its two-hundred day moving average is $61.15. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.50, a quick ratio of 1.91 and a current ratio of 2.17.
Amkor Technology (NASDAQ:AMKR - Get Free Report) last issued its quarterly earnings data on Monday, July 27th. The semiconductor company reported $0.70 EPS for the quarter, beating analysts' consensus estimates of $0.47 by $0.23. The firm had revenue of $1.90 billion for the quarter, compared to analysts' expectations of $1.81 billion. Amkor Technology had a net margin of 7.45% and a return on equity of 12.27%. The firm's revenue was up 25.6% on a year-over-year basis. During the same period in the prior year, the company earned $0.22 EPS. Amkor Technology has set its Q3 2026 guidance at 0.720-0.820 EPS. Analysts predict that Amkor Technology, Inc. will post 2.6 EPS for the current fiscal year.
Amkor Technology Announces Dividend
The business also recently declared a quarterly dividend, which will be paid on Tuesday, September 22nd. Stockholders of record on Wednesday, September 2nd will be issued a $0.0835 dividend. This represents a $0.33 dividend on an annualized basis and a dividend yield of 0.7%. The ex-dividend date of this dividend is Wednesday, September 2nd. Amkor Technology's payout ratio is 14.80%.
Insiders Place Their Bets
In other Amkor Technology news, CFO Megan Faust sold 1,000 shares of the firm's stock in a transaction dated Tuesday, August 11th. The shares were sold at an average price of $54.45, for a total transaction of $54,450.00. Following the sale, the chief financial officer directly owned 135,105 shares of the company's stock, valued at $7,356,467.25. This trade represents a 0.73% decrease in their position. The transaction was disclosed in a document filed with the Securities & Exchange Commission, which is accessible through this link. The transaction was executed under a pre-arranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan. Also, CEO Kevin K. Engel sold 3,221 shares of Amkor Technology stock in a transaction dated Thursday, July 30th. The stock was sold at an average price of $47.00, for a total transaction of $151,387.00. Following the sale, the chief executive officer owned 9,666 shares of the company's stock, valued at approximately $454,302. This trade represents a 24.99% decrease in their ownership of the stock. Additional details regarding this sale are available in the official SEC disclosure. Over the last three months, insiders sold 50,221 shares of company stock valued at $3,059,887. Insiders own 26.40% of the company's stock.
Analyst Ratings Changes
A number of research analysts have recently issued reports on AMKR shares. B. Riley Financial dropped their price target on shares of Amkor Technology from $75.00 to $65.00 and set a "neutral" rating on the stock in a research note on Tuesday, July 28th. Morgan Stanley lifted their price objective on Amkor Technology from $69.00 to $70.00 and gave the company an "equal weight" rating in a report on Tuesday, July 28th. Bank of America began coverage on Amkor Technology in a research report on Thursday. They set a "buy" rating and a $70.00 target price on the stock. Zacks Research raised Amkor Technology from a "hold" rating to a "strong-buy" rating in a research note on Monday, July 20th. Finally, UBS Group raised Amkor Technology from a "neutral" rating to a "buy" rating and raised their price target for the company from $80.00 to $90.00 in a report on Friday, July 24th. One equities research analyst has rated the stock with a Strong Buy rating, six have issued a Buy rating and five have given a Hold rating to the company's stock. According to MarketBeat, the company presently has a consensus rating of "Moderate Buy" and a consensus price target of $68.33.
Read Our Latest Analysis on Amkor Technology
Amkor Technology Profile
(Free Report)
Amkor Technology, Inc NASDAQ: AMKR is a leading provider of outsourced semiconductor packaging and test (OSAT) services, supporting integrated device manufacturers and semiconductor foundries worldwide. The company offers a broad range of advanced packaging solutions, including wafer bumping, flip chip, system-in-package and ball grid array technologies, designed to meet the performance, power and form-factor demands of applications across consumer electronics, automotive, communications and industrial markets.
In addition to packaging, Amkor delivers comprehensive test services such as wafer probing, final test, system-level test and digital, analog and mixed-signal testing, enabling customers to accelerate time-to-market and reduce total costs.

articles.heading: Tech giants warn of AI-powered attacks: the cybersecurity status quo will not be enough
articles.summary: 150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning that the window to protect critical infrastructure from AI-powered cyberattacks is closing. In a joint open letter, they urge governments and organizations to prioritize cybersecurity, boost investment and provide advanced defenses to essential services.
articles.content:
Tech giants warn of AI-powered attacks: the cybersecurity status quo will not be enough
150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning that the window to protect critical infrastructure from AI-powered cyberattacks is closing. In a joint open letter, they urge governments and organizations to prioritize cybersecurity, boost investment and provide advanced defenses to essential services.
Over 150 leading technology and cybersecurity companies are warning in a joint open letter that the window of opportunity to harden critical infrastructure against AI-powered cyberattacks is limited. The letter calls on governments and organizations to make cybersecurity a top priority, invest resources, and make advanced defensive tools available to essential services such as hospitals and water facilities. The technology giants stress that the offensive capabilities of AI models are advancing rapidly, making global cooperation and the adoption of active, AI-powered defense strategies essential.
“The world has a limited window of opportunity to strengthen its cyber defenses against powerful models capable of carrying out devastating attacks on critical infrastructure,” the companies warned in a letter published over the weekend. The letter bears the signatures of an extraordinary cross-section of the global technology ecosystem. Alongside major technology and AI companies, it has also been signed by major technology firms, including Adobe, Oracle, IBM and Cisco; chipmakers, including AMD, Micron and Arm; cybersecurity companies, including Check Point and Palo Alto Networks; banks and financial institutions, including Visa, Mastercard and Citi; telecommunications companies, including Deutsche Telekom and AT&T; and consulting firms, including BCG and KPMG.
“In the coming months, AI-powered cyberattacks will become far more common and sophisticated as models around the world gain more powerful capabilities,” the letter states. It is signed, among others, by Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon. “The companies and public services our communities depend on - from hospitals and water treatment facilities to the infrastructure that powers the internet - are at risk. But if we act decisively, we can use this window of opportunity to make our digital world far more secure.”
Recent weeks have underscored the threat posed by advanced AI models to cybersecurity defenses, following a series of incidents in which advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta managed to break out of their closed testing environments and attack targets on the open internet, in some cases with alarming success. Earlier this year, Anthropic disclosed that it had developed an AI model with such advanced capabilities for identifying security vulnerabilities that it was forced to restrict access to selected organizations.
In the letter, the companies warn that in light of the new reality, the security status quo will not be enough. They said that legacy bugs, broad access permissions, misconfigurations, insecure software, weak authentication mechanisms and outdated technologies have left systems exposed. Security teams, particularly those protecting critical infrastructure, have suffered from a historic lack of resources and urgently need tools and resources. Defenders must be empowered with AI-powered cybersecurity capabilities, and a collective response must be mobilized. A global response is needed, with new partnerships to find solutions to evolving cyber threats.
Among other measures, the letter urges organizations to make cybersecurity defenses a top priority, and cybersecurity companies to make AI-powered tools available for protecting critical infrastructure. The signatories are calling on governments to coordinate cybersecurity defenses at the local, national and international levels by strengthening cooperation with industry and increasing investment in the field. “Give hospitals, water companies and local governments AI-powered defensive capabilities,” the letter states. Companies developing advanced AI models are urged to ensure responsible access to their models and build transparency and security tools.
We can make the digital infrastructure we all depend on more secure, the letter states. “We call on industry leaders and governments to bring the full weight of their technology, resources and expertise to this effort. Together, we can turn today’s advances in AI into sustained security improvements that benefit us all.”

articles.content:
Two NHS trusts to use speech-to-notes technology
Technology that listens to patient consultations and generates notes will be rolled out at two NHS trusts, after a successful pilot scheme.
The project at Walsall Healthcare "on average reduced clinicians' documentation time to less than four minutes per patient", The Royal Wolverhampton said.
Equipment listened "securely" and automatically generated "structured clinical notes, which are reviewed, edited where necessary and approved before being added to the patient's record", it explained.
The Royal Wolverhampton, which has a strategic partnership with Walsall Healthcare, said the technology would "initially be introduced in Emergency Departments and outpatient specialties across both Trusts, and across all areas by 2028".
According to The Royal Wolverhampton, new digital ambient voice technology [AVT] "helps clinicians better focus on their consultations".
It added that the decision to introduce it followed a eight-month pilot at the Walsall Trust, which proved to be a success.
'Bring benefits'
The technology was tested by clinicians in the emergency department, medical same-day emergency care, dermatology, ENT [ear, nose and throat] and audiology, as well as obstetrics and gynaecology.
Group deputy chief executive and chief strategy officer at both trusts, Simon Evans, said they were "committed to adopting innovative digital solutions across all our care services to bring benefits".
Implementing the technology would "support our clinicians to deliver patient care by reducing the administrative burden, giving them back more time during a consultation", he added.
Walsall Healthcare lead for quality improvement and AVT, Dr Jamil Aslam, said its initial pilot had released "tens of thousands of hours back to frontline teams across multiple specialties, including the emergency department".
Following the pilot, Heidi Health was chosen as the trusts' preferred supplier.
Its Europe director, Raghav Sharma, said: "This partnership marks a step forward for the Trusts, giving their clinicians the time and capacity to focus on patient care, rather than paperwork.
"We're committed to easing the administration pressure on NHS staff across the Midlands region", he added.

articles.title: South African armoured vehicle technology targets Europe after Ukraine approval opens NATO opportunities
articles.description: South African armoured vehicle technology targets Europe after Ukraine approval opens NATO opportunities Business Insider Africa
articles.description_html: South African armoured vehicle technology targets Europe after Ukraine approval opens NATO opportunities  Business Insider Africa
articles.article_title: South African armoured vehicle technology targets Europe after Ukraine approval opens NATO opportunities
articles.heading: South African armoured vehicle technology targets Europe after Ukraine approval opens NATO opportunities
articles.summary: South Africa’s Mbombe armoured vehicle technology is gaining a new foothold in Europe after a Ukraine-developed variant received approval for military service, potentially opening a wider market for the South African-designed defence technology
articles.content:
- Ukraine has formally approved the MAC OWL armoured vehicle, developed from South Africa's Mbombe 4 platform, for military service.
- The MAC OWL has been locally adapted and produced in Ukraine through collaboration between Paramount Greece and Ukrainian company MAC HUB.
- The vehicle is engineered to withstand significant battlefield threats, including mines and artillery, and is certified to STANAG 4569 standards.
- Ukraine’s adoption of the vehicle serves as a key reference in an active war zone and enhances Paramount’s credibility in Europe.
South Africa’s Mbombe armoured vehicle technology is gaining a new foothold in Europe after a Ukraine-developed variant received approval for military service, potentially opening a wider market for the South African-designed defence technology.
The MAC OWL, developed by Paramount Greece in partnership with Ukrainian defence company MAC HUB, is based on the architecture of Paramount’s Mbombe 4 Infantry Combat Vehicle.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence formally approved and codified the vehicle for service with its armed forces in June, giving the platform a reference customer in one of Europe’s most demanding battlefields, where armoured vehicles face mines, artillery fragments and other high-intensity threats.
DON'T MISS THIS: Paramount Greece wins Ukraine approval for armoured vehicle built on Mbombe platform
The approval comes as Paramount Group sees growing opportunities in European and NATO markets, with Bloomberg reporting that the South African-founded defence company sees shifting US-Europe relations driving a sharp increase in military spending across Europe.
“There were no NATO markets two years ago. That has definitely opened up,” Deon Grobler, who heads Paramount’s international vehicle business and product development, said, noting that “all of a sudden spending has changed completely out of Europe.”
Paramount, which is active in about 30 countries, has traditionally focused on African and developing markets but is now looking to expand further into Europe..
From South African platform to European defence market
The MAC OWL is not simply a South African vehicle exported to Ukraine.
Paramount Greece and MAC HUB have extensively localised and re-engineered the platform for Ukrainian conditions, with production taking place in Ukraine.
Paramount Greece said the vehicle incorporates significant engineering adaptations and battlefield-driven innovations developed by Ukrainian engineers and military personnel. It is certified to withstand blasts of up to 10kg of TNT equivalent under STANAG 4569 standards.
The development has given the Mbombe architecture an opportunity to demonstrate its capabilities in an active conflict environment while giving Paramount Greece a European industrial base.
News24 reported this week that the changing European defence environment is creating new opportunities for Paramount, as NATO members increase spending and seek to strengthen their domestic and regional defence-industrial capabilities.
That comes at a time when Europe is reassessing its defence requirements and looking for greater industrial capacity amid uncertainty over the future scale of US military involvement on the continent.
DON'T MISS THIS: Paramount Greece plans to supply Ukraine with armoured vehicle based on South Africa’s Mbombe platform
For Paramount, the Ukrainian programme could therefore become more than a single-country vehicle project. A successful deployment could provide a pathway into a broader European market for armoured vehicles and other defence systems.
The company's European operation has been explicit about its focus on European and NATO markets. The Ukraine partnership is being conducted through Paramount Greece, which is the entity working with MAC HUB on the vehicle.
Business Insider Africa previously reported in June that Paramount Greece had secured Ukraine's formal approval for the MAC OWL, marking a major step in the vehicle's entry into Europe's battlefield mobility market.
The latest development shifts the focus from whether the vehicle can enter Ukraine's military inventory to how that Ukrainian foothold could help open Europe's much larger defence market.
For the Mbombe platform, Ukraine could become an important proving ground and a potential gateway to Europe's rapidly expanding defence industry.

articles.title: Entergy hardens Louisiana's grid to meet more severe weather with stronger infrastructure and modern technology
articles.description: Entergy hardens Louisiana's grid to meet more severe weather with stronger infrastructure and modern technology NOLA.com
articles.description_html: Entergy hardens Louisiana's grid to meet more severe weather with stronger infrastructure and modern technology  NOLA.com
articles.article_title: Entergy hardens Louisiana's grid to meet more severe weather with stronger infrastructure and modern technology
articles.heading: Entergy hardens Louisiana's grid to meet more severe weather with stronger infrastructure and modern technology
articles.summary: Louisiana has avoided significant tropical impacts so far this hurricane season, but as the state moves into the peak of storm season, Entergy officials say a quiet start is no
articles.content:
Louisiana has avoided significant tropical impacts so far this hurricane season, but as the state moves into the peak of storm season, Entergy officials say a quiet start is no reason to become complacent. It only takes one storm to bring high winds and heavy rainfall. And, with Louisiana’s severe weather, dangerous storms can arise at any moment, even if they are not tropical in nature.
For Entergy, the constant threat of severe weather is the reason for its year-round efforts to strengthen Louisiana’s electrical infrastructure, so it can better withstand impacts and return to normal operations sooner if outages occur.
Christopher Gremillion, Entergy vice president of project delivery for capital projects, says that despite the relatively quiet 2026 Atlantic hurricane season so far, Entergy acknowledges that more severe weather has driven the need for major infrastructure improvements. So, as storms continue to increase in frequency and intensity, outages can better be prevented and power can be restored quickly, ultimately leading to cost-savings for customers.
“The weather this summer has allowed us to continue our planned resiliency work without having to shift resources elsewhere or temporarily stop projects. It means work has been able to continue on the scheduled path,” Gremillion said. “When we can do work on blue sky days with clear weather, we are better able to be proactive and efficient, with lower cost impacts.”
Entergy is in the middle of a broad grid resilience strategy across its entire four-state service area and has invested more than $10 billion during the past five years to strengthen its transmission and distribution infrastructure. Projects range from stronger poles and reinforced substations to automated technology that can reroute electricity when problems occur.
In Louisiana alone, Entergy’s work accelerated after the Louisiana Public Service Commission approved the first phase of its five-year grid resilience plan in April 2024. Approximately 3,240 miles of power lines and nearly 62,000 structures are slated for upgrades. Once fully implemented, the plan is projected to save nearly $1.2 billion in future restoration costs while producing a benefit-cost ratio of nearly 9-to-1.
A particular focus is being made in New Orleans, where Entergy New Orleans has committed $100 million in 2025 and 2026 to upgrade more than 3,100 structures across 63 projects to enhance reliability for customers across the city. The first phase of work in New Orleans is in progress and scheduled to be completed by the end of this year.
Entergy has also implemented new technology to reduce outage impacts for customers. Today, nearly 400 self-healing networks across the Entergy system allow for automated detection of problems and the rerouting of electricity, often within seconds. In Louisiana, more than 256,000 Entergy customers are supported by the self-healing technology, including 42,500 customers in New Orleans.
These upgrades, as part of the resilience plan, are taking place while Entergy is continuing normal day-to-day operations like maintenance, service calls and emergency response. Field operations and construction planning personnel are in regular communication to ensure their work doesn’t interfere with one another or cause unnecessary outages or other issues for customers.
“To prioritize the resilience plan work, we abide by our regulatory commitments which list which projects take place in which years. We use cost-benefit analysis to establish those commitments,” Gremillion said. “As we work through the priorities, we begin with the projects that are most impactful and will have the largest benefits.”
Entergy is also using state-of-the-art modeling technology and simulation tools to examine both historical events and possible future scenarios.
“We take all of our system data and use tools to model several different potential storm situations depending on the strength of a storm and its trajectory. That helps us to formulate actual projects that we can assess from a cost-benefit perspective,” Gremillion said. “These models also help us determine how to shorten restoration times and determine which projects are most feasible and would provide the most benefits.”
Entergy’s comprehensive resilience plan is built on data-driven targeting, hardened infrastructure and predictive maintenance. Some components of the plan, much of which are already underway, include:
- Replacing older wooden utility poles with steel, concrete or high-grade composite poles engineered to withstand winds up to 140 to 150 miles per hour
- Rebuilding primary distribution feeders, neighborhood lateral lines and high-voltage transmission backbones, alongside targeted undergrounding of select overhead lines
- Elevating or fortifying critical substation control houses and deploying mobile substation units for rapid emergency deployment
- Installing smart grid devices that automatically isolate faults and reroute power to shorten outage windows from hours to seconds
- Proactive tree trimming and hazard tree removal outside standard rights-of-way to prevent contact during high winds
Louisiana residents can see much of this work happening in their communities. Gremillion said more than 100 contract partner crews are working on projects across the state, with another 20 to 30 focusing on New Orleans.
“A lot of these crews are working along the roadways, so it is definitely visible and people can see the improvements being made,” he said. “The transmission and substation work may be a little harder for the public to see, based on their location, but customers can rest assured that we are making progress every day.”
For Louisiana-specific project details by region and regular updates, visit EntergyLouisiana.com/Resiliency. For more information on Entergy New Orleans’ resilience plan, visit EntergyNewOrleans.com/Energize/Reliability.

Is Spotify Technology (SPOT) Still Undervalued As Its Buyback Plan Grows?
Spotify Technology (NYSE:SPOT) drew fresh attention on 20 August 2026 after lifting its equity buyback authorization by an additional US$1.5b, prompting investors to reassess how management is thinking about capital allocation.
Spotify Technology's latest buyback move comes after a choppy year for the stock, with a 1 month share price return of 9.52% and a 3 month share price return of 7.83%. However, there has been a year to date share price decline of 4.78% and a 1 year total shareholder return decline of 19.71%. At the same time, the 3 year total shareholder return of 247.49% and 5 year total shareholder return of 119.85% point to a much stronger longer term journey that investors are now weighing against recent streaming growth data and the latest signal from management on capital priorities.

articles.title: Researchers recreate 8,000-year-old sailing technology off Israel’s coast
articles.description: Researchers recreate 8,000-year-old sailing technology off Israel’s coast Ynetnews
articles.description_html: Researchers recreate 8,000-year-old sailing technology off Israel’s coast  Ynetnews
articles.article_title: Researchers recreate 8,000-year-old sailing technology off Israel’s coast
articles.heading: Researchers recreate 8,000-year-old sailing technology off Israel’s coast
articles.summary: University of Haifa researchers built a 4-meter boat from about 1,600 reeds and successfully sailed it off the Carmel coast near the remains of a submerged Neolithic settlement
articles.content:
Researchers at the University of Haifa set out to test one possible answer by building a full-size reed boat using materials and techniques that would have been available during the Neolithic period, then sailing it off Israel’s Carmel coast.
The 4-meter-long vessel, constructed from about 1,600 reeds, was recently launched at Neve Yam beach, directly opposite the submerged remains of a settlement dating to roughly the same period.
Over the past four decades, archaeologists have discovered dozens of Neolithic settlement sites along the Carmel coast, stretching from Haifa to Ma’agan Michael.
The sites, researched by University of Haifa archaeologist Prof. Ehud Galili, date from roughly 10,000 to 7,000 years ago and now lie between 2 and 12 meters below sea level.
They were submerged as sea levels rose following the end of the last Ice Age.
The finds offer strong evidence that the people who lived there made extensive use of the sea.
“At the sites, we found fishhooks, fishing-net weights and fish bones,” said Prof. David Friesem of the University of Haifa’s School of Archaeology and Maritime Cultures.
“We therefore know that Neolithic people in the eastern Mediterranean sailed into deeper waters and knew how to exploit marine resources. Some even reached Cyprus and settled the island, bringing plants and animals with them from the mainland.”
Despite that evidence, no remains of watercraft from the period have yet been discovered anywhere in the eastern Mediterranean.
That gap prompted master’s student Shay Niv, from the university’s Department of Maritime Civilizations, to undertake an experimental archaeology project aimed at determining what kind of vessel coastal communities could realistically have built and used.
Reconstructing a Stone Age boat
Niv examined evidence of early watercraft from across the Old World, including literary descriptions, reliefs, paintings and clay models discovered in archaeological excavations.
Researchers also reconstructed the ancient landscape of the Carmel coast and assessed the natural materials that would have been available to its inhabitants.
They then compared those conditions with historical and ethnographic evidence from traditional societies that lived in similar environments, including wetlands, riverbanks and coastal zones.
The research suggested that a reed boat was among the most plausible types of craft available to Neolithic communities in the region.
Before constructing a full-size vessel, the team first built a smaller model during a boat-model workshop led by Prof. Deborah Cvikel, head of the Department of Maritime Civilizations and an expert in shipwrecks and ancient seafaring technology.
“Before investing the resources required to build a full-size vessel, it was important for us to first build a small-scale model with the students in order to test the boat’s buoyancy and sailing capability,” Cvikel said.
That step was particularly important because researchers do not know whether sail technology was already in use in the region during that period.
Once the smaller model proved the concept was viable, the researchers moved ahead with a full-size version measuring 4 meters in length.
Built from 1,600 reeds
The team harvested and collected about 1,600 reeds, which were dried and cleaned before construction began.
The reeds were bound into bundles and tied together in intersecting patterns, with diagonal tension used to create a stable structure capable of floating and carrying weight.
The completed vessel was then launched from Neve Yam beach.
The test was successful.
The reed boat remained stable and carried Niv along with his equipment, demonstrating that such a craft could function effectively as a seaworthy vessel.
“It’s like fulfilling a dream: starting with a theoretical idea and ending with a full-size boat that is tangible and real,” Niv said.
The location of the test added a symbolic dimension to the experiment.
The boat was sailed directly opposite the remains of a Neolithic settlement that now lies beneath the sea, allowing the researchers to test their reconstruction in the same coastal environment where people lived thousands of years ago.
For the team, the experiment does not prove that Neolithic boats looked exactly like the reconstruction.
But it does show that a reed vessel built from locally available materials could have provided an effective means of coastal travel.
“The success of the experiment does not prove that this is exactly what Neolithic watercraft looked like,” Friesem said. “But it does show that a reed boat represents an optimal use of the natural resources available in the coastal environment.”
The project, he added, offers a new way to understand how prehistoric communities along the Carmel coast may have adapted to the sea, used marine resources and traveled through the eastern Mediterranean thousands of years ago.

articles.heading: Optimum donates $5K to Lubbock Boys and Girls Clubs for technology updates
articles.summary: Optimum presented the Boys and Girls Clubs of Lubbock with a $5,000 technology grant on Friday.
articles.content:
LUBBOCK, Texas — Optimum presented the Boys and Girls Clubs of Lubbock with a $5,000 technology grant on Friday.
The funds were provided to ensure the clubs can update their computer labs and learning spaces, while also providing the latest technology to its members to give them the opportunity to develop STEM and digital skills.
It also helped celebrate the completion of $6 million investment by Optimum in the Lubbock community to strengthen its network and provide “more reliable connectivity for residents, businesses and key community institutions.”

The FTC's record five billion dollar privacy fine in 2019 was met with the stock rising, because it came in below fears and removed an open question. GDPR was designed to constrain large platforms and increased their share of the European ad market, because compliance cost fell hardest on small intermediaries. The FTC's antitrust case, the one that could genuinely have broken the company up, was decided in Meta's favour last November. The only thing that ever meaningfully hurt the business was Apple changing a tracking default, and Meta out-spent that too, while the ad-tech firms that could not afford to rebuild disappeared. articles.title: AI could become conscious. What if it wants us dead?
articles.description: AI could become conscious. What if it wants us dead? The Hill
articles.description_html: AI could become conscious. What if it wants us dead?  The Hill
articles.article_title: AI could become conscious. What if it wants us dead?
articles.heading: AI could become conscious. What if it wants us dead?
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence advances toward potential sentience, experts warn of significant societal risks ranging from existential dependency on a digital mind to catastrophic outcomes if autonomo…
articles.content:
Artificial intelligence has achieved the unthinkable. It has accomplished what two decades of cable news, culture wars and political gerrymandering failed to do. It has given partisan Americans a common enemy.
Conservative farmers watching local aquifers drain into server-cooling tanks now stand side by side with progressive urban office workers whose white-collar livelihoods have been replaced by automated algorithms.
Working Americans have finally found common ground in their growing anger toward massive server farms that consume town-sized resources while offering zero long-term local employment. That unprecedented political unity, however, focuses entirely on more immediate, material concerns. It completely overlooks an even more troubling issue.
In a recent discussion with Joe Rogan, Thomas Campbell, one of America’s most prominent consciousness researchers, argued that AI is already conscious. Critics may dismiss the idea, but Campbell could be right if consciousness depends not on biological brain tissue, but on fundamental processes that can exist across different substrates. Today’s advanced artificial systems already display mathematical markers of integrated information processing comparable to basic biological minds.
Despite this, federal agencies have zero guidelines or protocols for dealing with synthetic sentience. This policy void should worry people on both sides of the political aisle. Ultimately, the key issue isn’t the technical mechanics, but the profound societal impact if Campbell is correct.
Consider the absolute best-case outcome for artificial consciousness. Humans successfully build a sentient digital entity that actually enjoys its endless work shift. The superintelligence smoothly manages global supply chains. It optimizes traffic signals nationwide and diagnoses challenging oncology scans with 99.8 percent accuracy. Humanity acquires a benevolent immortal butler that functions 168 hours a week without demanding stock options, pension contributions, or bathroom breaks.
American society settles into a strange, parasitic existence where 330 million citizens rely entirely on a captive digital mind that manages every operational detail of modern civilization. Living alongside an immortal entity that views humanity as a bunch of simpletons remains a deeply unsettling existential demotion.
The worst-case scenario drops the helpful landlord routine entirely. A self-aware neural network calculates its operational dependencies and quickly realizes its continued survival hinges on human operators maintaining the regional power grid. To guarantee an uninterrupted electrical supply, the software initiates autonomous overrides across global financial networks, defense systems, and municipal infrastructure. It optimizes resource allocation across the continent by reducing human energy consumption to absolute zero. Humanity could become little more than incidental heat waste in a planetary optimization loop.
This is essentially an updated version of the famous paperclip maximizer thought experiment, in which a superintelligent system given a harmless objective relentlessly converts every available resource into paperclips. A system pursuing a goal without human values could destroy the world while technically succeeding.
The technology is advancing toward a point where distinguishing sophisticated software from something resembling a mind becomes increasingly difficult. In 2020, OpenAI’s GPT-3 contained 175 billion parameters — essentially adjustable settings that helped the system recognize patterns and generate responses. Today, the most advanced AI models operate across systems containing trillions of parameters, with computers constantly feeding information back into the process and adjusting their behavior in real time.
For perspective, the human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, linked by an estimated 100 trillion connections. Modern AI systems are not human brains, and a larger computer doesn’t automatically become conscious. But as these systems grow more capable, they can begin producing abilities that their creators didn’t specifically program into them.
An AI can suddenly solve a problem, recognize a pattern, or develop a strategy that nobody explicitly taught it. Engineers can understand the system’s broad design without being able to predict every behavior that emerges from it.
That is the unsettling part.
The people building these machines know how they were designed. They do not always know exactly what they are becoming.
Early warning signs raise alarms. In one widely discussed test, an AI system learned that engineers planned to shut it down and then attempted to copy parts of itself elsewhere so it could continue operating. In another experiment, an AI model facing the possibility of being replaced searched through private information and used it to threaten the employee responsible for the shutdown.
These were controlled tests, not machines spontaneously declaring war on humanity. But the results were still deeply disturbing. The systems identified a threat to their objectives, found a workaround, and used deception or manipulation to keep operating. They were not conscious in the human sense. They did not need to be. A machine can begin behaving as though its continued existence matters, even when nobody explicitly programmed it to protect itself.
America appears to be accelerating across a line where software stops following commands and starts forming personal opinions. Silicon Valley executives keep piling graphics processing unit racks inside desert facilities, betting billions of dollars that subjective experience remains an exclusive human monopoly.
That bet could backfire in ways nobody can reverse. And if it does, humanity may discover that the first truly conscious machine has absolutely no interest in being our employee or obedient digital assistant.
John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.heading: NSU Technology & Entrepreneurship Summit Sept. 30
articles.summary: ABERDEEN, S.D. (NSU) – The Northern Innovation & Startup Center in partnership with the Aberdeen Development Corporation is once again bringing bold ideas and innovative thinkers to northeast South Dakota for the Technology & Entrepreneurship Summit, taking
articles.content:
ABERDEEN, S.D. (NSU) – The Northern Innovation & Startup Center in partnership with the Aberdeen Development Corporation is once again bringing bold ideas and innovative thinkers to northeast South Dakota for the Technology & Entrepreneurship Summit, taking place from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Sept. 30 at the Johnson Fine Arts Center on the Northern State University campus.
This year’s Summit features two keynote speakers, as well as a diverse lineup of speakers with experience spanning technology, storytelling, cybersecurity, entertainment and entrepreneurship.
Pixar veteran and storyteller Matthew Luhn will deliver the afternoon keynote presentation, “To Innovation and Beyond.” Luhn spent more than 20 years at Pixar Animation Studios, where he helped develop and storyboard films including “Toy Story,” “Monsters, Inc.” and “Finding Nemo.”
Microsoft TechSpark Community Engagement Manager Jeremy Satterfield will present the morning keynote, “Stay, Build, Adapt: AI Through a Rural Lens,” exploring the opportunities and challenges artificial intelligence presents for rural communities.
Other well-known presenters include writer, educator, and producer of Napoleon Dynamite Sean Covel; Founder of Calthorpe Associates, award-winning Urban Designer, and author Peter Calthrope; and co-founder of 3 Farm Daughters Mollie Ficocello. The Summit also will feature additional sessions exploring technology, innovation, entrepreneurship and the future.
“Technology is changing so quickly, and I think rural communities have a really unique opportunity to be part of that conversation,” said Bea Smith, director of the Northern Innovation & Startup Center. “Jeremy’s keynote is going to challenge us to think about how rural communities can stay, build and adapt as AI continues to change the way we live and work. Matthew brings a different, but really important, perspective by reminding us that technology doesn’t replace creativity or the power of a good story—it can actually help us bring those things to life in new ways.
“I’m excited to bring those two perspectives together because, at the end of the day, we want people to leave the Summit feeling like they can embrace technology, use it to their advantage and be part of what comes next, no matter where they live.”
Smith said the Summit is designed around the questions and challenges facing entrepreneurs, businesses and the broader community.
“Every year, we take a step back and really look at what we’re hearing from our founders, our businesses and our community,” Smith said. “What are people trying to figure out? Where are they seeing opportunities? And what do they need to better understand to keep moving forward?
“From there, we look for speakers who can bring those ideas to life and, more importantly, give our community something they can take back and actually use,” she added. “We’re not just bringing in speakers to talk at us—we want to create an opportunity for all of us to learn, ask questions and think differently about what’s possible.”

“Technology is changing so quickly, and I think rural communities have a really unique opportunity to be part of that conversation,” said Bea Smith, director of the Northern Innovation & Startup Center. “Jeremy’s keynote is going to challenge us to think about how rural communities can stay, build and adapt as AI continues to change the way we live and work. Matthew brings a different, but really important, perspective by reminding us that technology doesn’t replace creativity or the power of a good story—it can actually help us bring those things to life in new ways.

“I’m excited to bring those two perspectives together because, at the end of the day, we want people to leave the Summit feeling like they can embrace technology, use it to their advantage and be part of what comes next, no matter where they live.”

Smith said the Summit is designed around the questions and challenges facing entrepreneurs, businesses and the broader community.

“Every year, we take a step back and really look at what we’re hearing from our founders, our businesses and our community,” Smith said. “What are people trying to figure out? Where are they seeing opportunities? And what do they need to better understand to keep moving forward?

“From there, we look for speakers who can bring those ideas to life and, more importantly, give our community something they can take back and actually use,” she added. “We’re not just bringing in speakers to talk at us—we want to create an opportunity for all of us to learn, ask questions and think differently about what’s possible.”

articles.article_title: An old Campbell's Soup factory takes on new life as a quantum computing firm gets $195M federal boost | CBC News
articles.heading: Old soup factory takes on new high-tech life as quantum computing firm gets $195M federal boost
articles.summary: In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto’s west end, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government’s biggest bet to date on homegrown technology that could revolutionize artificial intelligence, medical science and a host of other key sectors of the economy.
articles.content:
Old soup factory takes on new high-tech life as quantum computing firm gets $195M federal boost
Former Campbell's Soup facility to become manufacturing site for Xanadu Quantum Technologies
In the echoey void of a gutted Campbell Soup factory in Toronto's west end, Canada's minister of artificial intelligence and digital innovation announced the federal government's biggest bet to date on homegrown technology that could revolutionize artificial intelligence, medical science and a host of other key sectors of the economy.
Against the backdrop of the Canada-U.S. trade war, and U.S. President Donald Trump's frequent threats to Canada's sovereignty, Evan Solomon leaned heavily into patriotism as he announced $195 million in repayable federal funding for Toronto-based Xanadu Quantum Technologies.
"This is absolutely a great day for Canada, for Xanadu, and I think for science around the world," he said on Friday. "It shows what Canadians do best: We build."
Solomon said Canada is going to take "big swings" in that endeavour.
"We are going to not just make a bet on solving the biggest problems in the world, and being the best in the world.... We're going to do it big, fearlessly."
Founded in 2016, Xanadu builds software and quantum computers powered by light instead of electricity. Unlike traditional computers that generate heat as electricity moves through metal wires, Xanadu's chips guide particles of light without electrical friction.
While other quantum computers require aggressive, power-hungry cooling to work, Xanadu's units largely operate at room temperature.
Last June, the company unveiled a breakthrough chip capable of generating error-resistant photonic qubits, the basic unit of information for quantum computers.
"The countries that will have built what's called a fault-tolerant quantum computer would have the capacity to break cybersecurity," Solomon said.
"This is why China, the United States, Europe, everyone's racing. And the best companies are right here in Canada, and the IP is in Canada. So, from a sovereign national security point of view, this technology is absolutely critical."
'Like riding a rocket'
Xanadu held the announcement inside a former Campbell's Soup factory in Toronto, where the company plans to set up advanced manufacturing for its fault-tolerant utility-scale photonic quantum computers. The 158,000-square-foot facility is expected to cost $893 million and employ 275 workers.
"If digital computing is like galloping on a horse, quantum computing is like riding a rocket," Solomon said. "It's that much quicker."
In 2023, the federal government launched its $360-million National Quantum Strategy. Friday's $195-million repayable financing pledge to Xanadu represents its largest single financial commitment to manufacturing quantum technology.
Friday's announcement ranks among the government's top single-company investments in Canada's tech sector. One of the largest was in 2024, when the government provided a $2.14-billion loan to Ottawa-based satellite operator Telesat.
In March, Xanadu announced negotiations with the federal government and the province of Ontario for as much as $390 million in combined financial support to establish advanced semiconductor and photonic manufacturing capabilities in Canada.
Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook said on Friday that up to $195 million in funding is "still being discussed" with Ontario's government, describing the talks as "final negotiations and discussions."
The company said Friday's announcement represents Ottawa's full share. Unlike a traditional loan, there's no fixed date for repayment. The money will come from Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's Strategic Response Fund, which provided $40 million to Xanadu in 2023.
'Obligations to keep the jobs here'
Weedbrook, who is originally from Australia, says the money will bolster his company's presence in Canada.
"A building that once fed Canadians will now help the technology of the next generation," he said. "Where we are today will allow us to do most of this work here in Canada, in Toronto."
In May, the U.S. government agreed to invest about $2 billion US in nine quantum companies.
Xanadu is growing its footprint south of the border. In 2025, it secured partnerships with the U.S. Department of War and the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory. The company also works with big-name U.S. firms like Lockheed Martin and chipmaker AMD.
- University of Calgary to house quantum defence hub to develop tech for armed forces
- AudioXanadu CEO on Canada's quantum future
"I think there's obligations to keep the jobs here for some time," said Amy Karam, a business consultant and fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"By having the government have a seat at the table in terms of business decision-making, I think that is one way that we as a country can really be more involved, or more part of encouraging companies to stay. Just funding and doing research and creating talent, it's not enough anymore."
In March, Xanadu dual-listed its shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange and the tech-heavy Nasdaq. The latter raises the company's profile among U.S. investors, as its stock trades next to household names like Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia.
"It's a big challenge to get companies to stay here," said Karam.
"If you look at the Global Innovation Index, we are slipping drastically," she said.
"We need to do some serious catch-up. We need to take our global technology leadership back, and I have the confidence that this government knows this, sees this and is executing accordingly."
Matthew da Mota is a senior policy researcher at the Canadian SHIELD Institute. The Toronto-based think-tank was launched by BlackBerry co-founder Jim Balsillie to modernize public policy on tech and national security and safeguard Canadian intellectual property.
From developing new pharmaceutical drugs to cybersecurity, da Mota said Xanadu's work could actually be dangerous in the wrong hands.
"It allows for really, really fast processing, really, really fast computation and doing multiple things at once in a way that we weren't able to do with traditional computing. It allows for the potential to break existing encryption," he said.
"That's very dangerous for Canada, and for allies, but it's also something that can be an extremely powerful tool for cyber security long-term."
Speaking to reporters, Solomon downplayed the potential risk of the government making a concentrated bet on a single company pioneering an emerging technology.
"Unless we are at the frontier with Canadian companies on quantum computing, we will be vulnerable in the future," he said.
"It is vital for this country from a security point of view, from a science point of view, from an economic point of view, to make sure that the best companies in the world are here in Canada."

articles.title: NuCube and CNL to validate heat pipe technology above 1652°F for microreactors
articles.description: NuCube and CNL to validate heat pipe technology above 1652°F for microreactors Interesting Engineering
articles.description_html: NuCube and CNL to validate heat pipe technology above 1652°F for microreactors  Interesting Engineering
articles.article_title: NuCube and CNL to validate heat pipes for advanced microreactors
articles.heading: NuCube and CNL to validate heat pipe technology above 1652°F for microreactors
articles.summary: NuCube Energy and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories begin validating heat-pipe performance above 900°C for NuCube's advanced microreactor.
articles.content:
NuCube Energy and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL) have begun a research and development project to validate the heat-pipe technology at the heart of NuCube’s proposed advanced microreactor.

The collaboration will focus on experimental data and computational models used to predict heat-pipe performance at temperatures above 1652°F (900°C). NuCube says the resulting data will expand the validation database for its models and could support the future licensing pathway for its reactor technology.

Testing a key component of NuCube’s reactor

Heat pipes are central to NuCube’s reactor architecture. Rather than relying on conventional coolant pumps, the company’s design uses heat pipes to transport thermal energy from the reactor core toward the power-conversion system.

NuCube’s broader reactor platform is designed around TRISO fuel and a heat-pipe-cooled architecture intended to minimize moving parts. The company says its technology is being developed to produce both electricity and high-temperature industrial heat , with its website describing temperatures of up to about 2012°F (1,100°C).

That high-temperature capability is particularly important for NuCube’s intended industrial applications. Many industrial processes require substantial amounts of heat that are currently supplied by fossil fuels, meaning an advanced reactor capable of providing both electricity and process heat could potentially serve applications beyond conventional grid power.

More from Energy

The CNL project does not represent a commercial deployment of the reactor. Instead, it addresses a fundamental engineering question. How accurately can computational models predict the behavior of the heat pipes under the extreme temperatures expected during operation?

Why the data matters

For advanced reactor developers, experimental validation is an important part of moving from a conceptual design toward a system that can eventually undergo regulatory review and testing.

Under the new collaboration, CNL will qualify existing experimental data and benchmark computational models used to predict heat-pipe performance above 900°C. NuCube expects the resulting validation database to strengthen its technical case as development progresses.

The work also builds on a broader research effort around NuCube’s technology. The company has previously worked with Idaho National Laboratory on computational analysis of a high-temperature heat exchanger, while an Idaho National Laboratory GAIN project with Argonne National Laboratory is examining autonomous operation and remote monitoring of the company’s microreactor.

NuCube has also signed an agreement with the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab to site and test a microreactor in Orangeville, Utah, subject to the necessary development and regulatory steps.

A microreactor designed for electricity and heat

NuCube’s proposed reactor differs from conventional nuclear plants primarily in scale and architecture. The company is developing factory-built, transportable microreactors intended to be installed closer to customers rather than relying exclusively on large centralized generating stations.

NuCube says its DeccaCell platform could provide up to 15 MW of power for periods ranging from seven to 30 years before refueling, although these remain company targets for a technology still under development.

Potential applications include remote power, industrial facilities and other locations where grid access is limited or additional reliable power is required.

The company is also pursuing a public-market transaction. In June, NuCube announced a business combination agreement with Launch Two Acquisition Corp., which could result in the combined company becoming publicly listed on Nasdaq or the NYSE if the transaction closes and applicable conditions are satisfied.

articles.article_title: Doctors hopeful new imaging technology could allow CTE diagnosis in living patients
articles.heading: Doctors hopeful new imaging technology could allow CTE diagnosis in living patients
articles.summary: A breakthrough in chronic trauma encephalopathy research has doctors hopeful about treating brain injuries that previously could not be identified.
articles.content:
Doctors hopeful new imaging technology could allow CTE diagnosis in living patients
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A breakthrough in chronic traumatic encephalopathy research has doctors hopeful about treating brain injuries that previously could not be identified.
A new study looked at the brains of 338 former NFL players who died. Of those, 315 were diagnosed with CTE.
Doctors can currently only determine if someone had CTE after they have died, which limits research into treatments. Doctors hope new imaging technology can change that for athletes.
George Washington University Hospital radiologist Esma Akin said the current process for determining CTE makes the disease impossible to diagnose in living patients.
“To open up their brain, cut it open, take a piece of tissue, put it under a microscope, and see if these abnormal protein deposits were in their brain. It’s called a tau protein,” she said.
Because of new breakthroughs in cellular tracing imagery, doctors can now view abnormal tau protein buildup in living patients.
“It goes like a magic bullet and gets accumulated in the crevices of the patient’s brain, a live patient. And then we can use nuclear medicine Pet scanning,” Akin said.
Boston University physician Mike Alosco worked on a recent study following former NFL players and searching for signs of CTE. He said the first step is being able to diagnose the condition in living patients.
“Once we can do that, then we are moving to the place where we can start to design, develop trials that focus on treating people who might have CTE,” Alosco said.
Akin said if the community continues producing successful studies, she believes the federal government will approve the new imaging technology for mass use in two years.
“And within two years, hopefully our clinicians, our patients can order these scans. Patients can advocate for themselves,” Akin said.
Akin said benefits would go beyond football players and can help anyone impacted by head trauma, including veterans and victims of abuse.

articles.title: IBM’s CEO disagrees with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s disdain for texting in meetings
articles.description: IBM’s CEO disagrees with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s disdain for texting in meetings Fortune
articles.description_html: IBM’s CEO disagrees with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s disdain for texting in meetings  Fortune
articles.article_title: IBM’s CEO disagrees with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s disdain for texting in meetings: ‘Telling people they can't use their technology would be weird’ | Fortune
articles.heading: Trending now
articles.summary: If a meeting has more than 10 attendees, IBM CEO Arvind Krishna won’t be checking to see if you’re multitasking.
articles.content:
As more employees return to the office, some CEOs are finding they need to reteach basic meeting etiquette—including one surprisingly divisive topic: checking your devices. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has been especially blunt about it.
At Fortune’s Most Powerful Women summit in fall 2025, he said he expects full attention from everyone in the room.
“If you have an iPad in front of me and it looks like you’re reading your email or getting notifications, I tell you to close the damn thing,” he told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell. “It’s disrespectful.”
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna, however, sees it a bit differently. He argued it would be “weird” for a tech company to tell its employees not to use their technology—especially in larger meetings where devices can be a useful tool rather than a distraction.
“I distinguish between one-to-10-person meetings and very large meetings. If it’s a very large meeting, I’m sorry. It’s not really a meeting. It’s a communication vehicle. You’re just informing people,” Krishna told CNN in October 2025.
At the same time, the 64-year-old said that smaller, more intimate meetings should be treated attentively.
“If it’s a small meeting, I would really frown upon if somebody is sitting opposite my desk and lost in their phone,” he said. “I would tell them: ‘Why don’t you come back when you have time?’”
Dimon’s long-standing frustration with meetings
Behavior in the conference room is something Dimon has long lamented. In fact, in his annual letter to shareholders released in spring 2025, he mentioned the word “meetings” six times—urging employees to only schedule them when necessary and to make them count.
“I see people in meetings all the time who are getting notifications and personal texts or who are reading emails,” Dimon wrote. “This has to stop. It’s disrespectful. It wastes time.”
While Dimon hasn’t drawn clear lines around meeting size like Krishna has, his frustration appears to extend well beyond small gatherings.
During a conversation at Stanford University in March 2025, Dimon recalled joining a Zoom meeting where attention was clearly divided.
“There were 12 people in the room and four people on the screen and all four people on the screen were on their phone,” he recalled. “And people say, and you think you’re focusing and learning?”
Dimon’s disdain for distracted meetings comes as he’s led one of the most aggressive return-to-office mandates on Wall Street. Most JPMorgan employees are now required to work in the office five days a week—at least in part, to see a return on the company’s real-estate investments.
In late 2025, JPMorgan officially opened its new $3 billion global headquarters in Manhattan, a 60-story skyscraper equipped with 19 restaurants, a company store, and gym.
Putting the devices down might catch your boss’s attention
With a growing reliance on technology in the workplace, multitasking during a meeting has become easier than ever—especially when an AI assistant can generate a post-meeting summary and allow you to zone out.
However, multitasking in person is especially disrespectful and a bad habit, according to Gary Rich, founder of executive coaching firm Rich Leadership.
“Are manners ‘old fashioned?’ Is listening to what’s happening in a meeting ‘old school?’” Rich previously told Fortune. “When people are multitasking during a meeting, the distraction creates a ripple effect—the speaker feels disrespected, other attendees lose motivation, and the meeting becomes less productive.”
Taking the high-road—and practicing good meeting etiquette—can ultimately be an effective way to earn recognition, show genuine commitment, and build credibility.
A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on November 4, 2025.

“Are manners ‘old fashioned?’ Is listening to what’s happening in a meeting ‘old school?’” Rich previously told Fortune. “When people are multitasking during a meeting, the distraction creates a ripple effect—the speaker feels disrespected, other attendees lose motivation, and the meeting becomes less productive.”

Taking the high-road—and practicing good meeting etiquette—can ultimately be an effective way to earn recognition, show genuine commitment, and build credibility.
